name: Carla Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential and won't be traced back to you. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine, thank you. I'll be honest, I almost said no, because every time someone wants to talk about AI it ends with me being told I'm a dinosaur at twenty-seven.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior designer at a four-person studio in the old mill building on Station Road. We do posters, programmes and logos for theatres, festivals and small charities, mostly. I start with coffee and a sketchbook, because I still draw every idea by hand before it goes near the screen, then it's layouts in the afternoon and a fight with a printer about ink colours by four. I love the moment a poster comes back from the press and it's right. What wears me out is the pay: I earn less than designers in the city, my partner Noor works part time at the library, and we've got maybe three weeks of rent put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say I told you so, a bit smugly, in the studio group chat. Online I'd post something about how real design was never going to be replaced by a button. My boss would laugh, because she's been half expecting it to replace me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays the same, which isn't all good news. I'm still on lower pay, still three weeks from trouble if a theatre pays late. The tech didn't come for me, but the rent still does, every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and stop losing sleep over the tech news. I'd push my boss for the pay rise she promised in spring, maybe two thousand a year. And I'd try to put fifty a month aside so one late invoice doesn't wreck us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly. But a tired kind of relief, because the money worry was there long before any of this. Nothing about AI flopping makes the boiler at our flat any younger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a theatre paying late could wreck you. Has that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter the Playhouse took eleven weeks to pay us, and the studio held my overtime back until the money came in. Noor and I ate a lot of lentils that December. When a theatre pays late, I eat lentils, and no clever software was ever going to change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If routine tasks do get automated, which parts of your week would that touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Resizing, mostly. When a festival wants one poster in nine sizes for buses, phones and banners, that's a whole day of boring work. If software did that, I wouldn't cry, as long as the day it frees up isn't the day they stop paying me for.

say: I'd tell the studio **real design** was never going to come from a button.
I'd post online that the **hype crowd** owed artists an apology.
think: My life stays the same, and that includes **lower pay** and a thin cushion.
A **late invoice** from one theatre still scares me more than any software.
do: Push my boss in spring for the **promised raise** of about two thousand a year.
Set aside **fifty a month** so one late payment can't sink the household.
Keep drawing by hand and **stop reading** the tech news at night.
feel: **Relief** that the hype passed, but a tired relief.
The **money worry** stays, because it was there before AI came up.
S0.quote: When a theatre pays late, I eat lentils, and no clever software was ever going to change that.
fieldNote: She treats **AI flopping** as a win but immediately turns to rent, pay and the boiler.
Her real pressure is **cash flow**: one late theatre payment already cost her a hard December.
She'd accept software doing **resizing work**, as long as it doesn't cut her paid hours.

steps.text: Ask her boss for the promised raise of about two thousand a year
Put fifty a month into a separate rent buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it loudly: this is theft dressed up as progress. These tools learned from designers' work without paying anyone, and now they're sold back to our clients. I'd be the one sharing every petition about artists' rights and asking why nobody regulated this first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm in trouble. A charity that paid us eight hundred for a poster will type a sentence into a generator and get something good enough for free. My boss would want me to use the tools, and I'd refuse, and I know how that ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd join the designers' union, which I've meant to do for two years, and get Noor to help me look at the actual numbers. I'd keep my hand-drawn work front and centre, maybe pitch the studio as the human-made option for theatres that care. I'd also start looking at teaching art at the college one evening a week, because that's the only other design work in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like watching the tide come in while I'm stood on the sand insisting I like the view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if your boss told you to start using the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say no the first time and probably give in the third time, because I can't afford to be proud with three weeks of savings. I hate admitting that. If my boss makes generators part of the job, I'll either learn them badly or lose the job, and I can't afford to lose the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the studio would you worry about besides yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our junior, Kit, who's twenty-two and does the resizing and social posts. That work is exactly what these tools eat first. I trained Kit, and I'd feel sick watching that job disappear while I'm still clinging to mine.

say: I'd call it **theft dressed up** as progress, built on unpaid artists' work.
I'd share every **petition** and ask why nobody regulated these tools first.
think: Charities paying **eight hundred** for a poster will settle for a free generator.
If I keep **refusing the tools**, I expect to lose my job before long.
do: Join the **designers' union** this month after two years of putting it off.
Pitch the studio to theatres as the **human-made** option.
Ask the college about teaching **one evening** a week.
feel: Sick, like watching the **tide come in** and pretending to enjoy it.
**Ashamed** that she'd probably give in to the tools for money.
S1.quote: If my boss makes generators part of the job, I'll either learn them badly or lose the job, and I can't afford to lose the job.
fieldNote: Her public line is **principled anger**; privately she admits she'd give in by the third time.
Thin savings make her **resistance** to the tools something she can't afford for long.
She worries for **the junior**, whose resizing work is first in line.

steps.text: Join the designers' union and pay the first month's fee
Pitch the studio to local theatres as hand-made design
Apply to teach one evening art class at the college
Sign petitions on artists' copyright and write to her MP

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what everyone would be saying: nobody voted for this. I'd be at whatever protest there was, holding a sign I'd drawn myself, which feels pathetic and also like the only thing I'd know how to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my career ends before I'm thirty. Design is screen work, all of it, so the 2028 date is my date, not 2031. The only bit of my job that's hands-on is mixing inks with the printer and that's not my job, that's his.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the printer, Mr Okafor, if he'd take me on part time, because he gets three more years before robots reach his press. I'd sign up for every bit of help the government offers and I wouldn't be ashamed of it. Noor and I would give up the flat and move in with her mum, who has a spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panic. I don't have a plan, I don't have money, and two years isn't long enough to make either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move in with Noor's mum. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, then kindly. Her mum would say yes before Noor finished asking, and I'd cry in the car afterwards. Moving into my partner's mum's spare room at twenty-nine is not the life I drew for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap before robots change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only through other people. The printer might get three more years, the sign-fitters too. I'd be trying to borrow a bit of their time, sweeping floors at the print shop if I had to.

say: I'd say **nobody voted** for this and turn up to every protest.
I'd carry a **hand-drawn sign**, because that's the only tool I trust.
think: My **design career** ends before I'm thirty, because all of it is screen work.
**2028** is my date; the extra robot years belong to the printer, not me.
do: Ask the printer for **part-time work** at the press before the date arrives.
Give up the flat and move into **Noor's mum's** spare room.
Claim every **government support** payment without shame.
feel: **Panic**, with no plan and no money to make one.
**Grief** for the life she'd sketched for herself.
S2.quote: Moving into my partner's mum's spare room at twenty-nine is not the life I drew for myself.
fieldNote: She sees immediately that **all her work** is thinking work, so the robot gap barely helps.
Her only plan borrows time from **hands-on people** around her, like the printer.
Unlike her public anger, her private reaction is **helplessness**, not fight.

steps.text: Ask the print shop owner for part-time work at the press
Give up the flat and move into her partner's mum's spare room
Apply for every government income support she qualifies for
Join protests against the speed of the rollout

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years and we'd better use them to write the rules. I'd be on at the union every week to push for a tax on the companies doing this, paid out to the people it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to thirty-two. That's long enough to see it, not long enough to dodge it. My design work still goes in 2031, just with a longer queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a printmaking course at the college now, screen printing and letterpress, because that's hands-on and gets the three extra years. I'd try to save properly, maybe a hundred a month, which means cutting the streaming and the takeaway Fridays. And I'd talk to Noor about whether we'd be better off somewhere cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but less frozen. Five years is enough to start something, even if I don't trust it to finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use AI tools. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. I'd learn enough to know what I'm up against, the way you'd read the contract that sacks you. Learning the tools wouldn't save my job, but at least I'd understand what replaced me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would cheaper mean, for you and Noor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor's from a market town two hours north where rent is half ours. There's no design work there at all, which is sort of the point by 2031. I'd rather be broke somewhere cheap than broke here.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to write the rules, so start now.
I'd push the union for a **tax on the companies**, paid to replaced workers.
think: Five years takes me to **thirty-two**, long enough to see it, not dodge it.
My **design work** still ends in 2031, just with a longer wait.
do: Start a **printmaking course** this year, because hands-on work gets three extra years.
Save about **a hundred a month** by cutting streaming and takeaway Fridays.
Talk to Noor about moving to her **cheaper hometown**.
feel: **Scared but less frozen** than with the two-year picture.
Doubtful that anything she starts will **last**.
S3.quote: I'd rather be broke somewhere cheap than broke here.
fieldNote: The extra time turns her **panic into planning**, but she still expects to lose her design job.
She'd learn the tools only to **understand the threat**, not to use them.
Her retraining choice uses the **three-year robot gap** deliberately.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening screen printing and letterpress course
Cancel streaming and takeaway Fridays to save a hundred a month
Plan a move to her partner's cheaper market town
Push the union to campaign for a tax on AI firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift and we'd be fools to waste it. I'd want design schools and unions planning now, not in 2035 when it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is real time. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, and I could have a second trade by then. I still don't think graphic design survives, but I might.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and do the printmaking course slowly, one evening a week, no panic. I'd help the union build a fund for retraining designers, because I'd rather organise than sulk. And I'd stop pretending I'll never touch the tools and try them on resizing jobs, so I'm not the last to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but like I can breathe. The fear's still there, it's just further down the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change any family plans for you and Noor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about kids around thirty-two. Ten years means those kids would be little when it all lands. I'd want to know there's a safety net before I bring a child into a world where my trade is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which is it, then: do you expect to be fine, or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not fine as a designer, fine as a person, maybe. With ten years, I'd have time to become a printmaker, a teacher, whatever's left. Ten years is the difference between losing a job and losing your footing.

say: I'd say **a decade** is a gift we'd be fools to waste.
I'd want unions and design schools **planning now**, not in 2035.
think: At **thirty-seven** I could have a second trade before the end arrives.
I still expect **graphic design** to go, but I'd have time to land.
do: Take the **printmaking course** one evening a week while keeping the studio job.
Help the union build a **retraining fund** for designers.
Try the tools on **resizing jobs** so she isn't the last to know.
feel: Still **uneasy**, but able to breathe with the threat further away.
S4.quote: Ten years is the difference between losing a job and losing your footing.
fieldNote: With ten years, she moves from **resistance to slow preparation**, even trying the tools.
**Family plans** for kids around thirty-two depend on a safety net existing first.
She still expects to lose **design income**, but believes she'd have control.

steps.text: Take the printmaking course one evening a week alongside her job
Help the designers' union set up a retraining fund
Try AI tools on resizing jobs at the studio
Hold off on children until a safety net is in place

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. Two years, no savings, a trade that's all screens. What would help is money in my hand while I retrain, not a leaflet, and a union strong enough to make the companies pay for it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the work itself, what it feels like to make it. When a theatre poster I drew goes up on the high street, people stop and look. I'd like someone to count that before deciding a machine can do it.

headlineQuote: When a theatre poster I drew goes up on the high street, people stop and look.
portrait: Carla is a **senior designer** at a four-person studio making posters and logos for theatres and charities.
She draws every idea by hand, **never uses AI**, and lives with her partner Noor on thin savings.
Her **money worry** predates AI: one late theatre payment already meant a winter of lentils.
In faster pictures she expects to **lose design work** and leans on family, union and government help.
With **ten years**, she plans printmaking, organising and even trying the tools on routine work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most: two years, no savings and a job that is all screen work.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** money in hand, not leaflets.
A **strong union** that makes AI companies pay for the transition.
